## At a glance

**Guiding question:** Which resource limits care in the scenario under study?\
**For:** trauma surgeons, anaesthetists and nurses who write or test a hospital's mass casualty plan, emergency
planners, analysts in hospital operations · **Prerequisites:** the difference between a forecast and a simulated
capacity change (@sec-b17); random draws and replications, as in
[Strategy in R: Monte Carlo Methods for Games](https://cttir.github.io/strategy-in-r/sec-monte-carlo.html)\
**In the course:** [W6 · Pharmacometrics, forecasting and simulation](https://cttir.github.io/clinical-data-science-in-r-course/lessons/w6-pharmacometrics-forecasting-simulation.html)
(required reading, as an alternative to @sec-b15) · **Data:** synthetic (generated in the chapter) ·
**Core reading time:** about 10 minutes

## Case and decision {#sec-b18-case}

A trauma surgeon chairs the working group that revises the hospital's plan for mass casualty incidents. Two proposals
compete for the first hour after an alert. One is to open a third operating room at once, which means stopping the
elective list in that room and calling in a second on-call team. The other is to equip a third resuscitation bay in the
emergency department, which is cheaper and does not cancel anyone's operation. The group asks an analyst for a
simulation. The surgeon's question is concrete: *in the scenario we consider likely, which resource limits care, and how
much waiting does each proposal remove for which patients?* The answer goes into the plan. A wrong choice costs time for
seriously injured patients in a real incident, and either choice has costs for elective patients and staff that the
plan must state openly.

## Core reading {#sec-b18-core}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Core reading** · required for W6 (alternative to @sec-b15) · about 10 minutes · ends before ‘Lab’
:::

```{r}
#| label: b18-run-lab-early
#| include: false
#| purl: false
#| ref.label: ["b18-events", "b18-model", "b18-checks", "b18-run", "b18-pairing"]
```

**What a simulation can claim.** A forecast (@sec-b17) predicts what will happen if nothing changes and can be checked
a week later. A capacity simulation answers a "what if" question about a change that has not been made, under an
assumed stream of patients. It cannot be checked against the outcome before a real incident. Its credibility rests on
three things that this chapter makes explicit: the input assumptions, the verification of the model logic, and a
plausibility check against external figures [@sargent2013validation].

**Discrete-event and agent-based models.** In a *discrete-event simulation* (DES), patients move through a fixed
pathway of resources (here: resuscitation bay, then operating room). The clock jumps from event to event: an arrival,
the start or end of a treatment. Queues form when a resource is busy, and a priority rule decides who goes next. The R
package `simmer` implements this approach [@ucar2019simmer]. In an *agent-based model*, individuals follow their own
rules and interact, for example staff who tire or clinicians who re-triage patients as they deteriorate (see
[Strategy in R: Agent-Based Models for Strategic Interaction](https://cttir.github.io/strategy-in-r/sec-agent-based-models.html)).
For a question about the capacity of a fixed pathway, DES is the simpler and more transparent choice.

**The scenario.** After an alert at time zero, 14 casualties who need urgent surgery arrive within three hours. About
40% are triaged red (immediate), the rest yellow (urgent but able to wait). Each patient first occupies one of two
resuscitation bays for about 30 minutes and then waits for an operating room. Operations take about two hours for red
and one and a half hours for yellow patients, with considerable spread. Red patients have priority at every step.
Three scenarios are compared: A, two operating rooms (the regular night set-up); B, three operating rooms; C, two
operating rooms and a third resuscitation bay. All numbers are *assumptions* for teaching. A real plan would take them
from the hospital's own records and from published series.

**Fix the events before comparing.** The most important design decision comes before any simulation is run. For each
of 200 replications, the list of arrival times, triage categories and treatment times is drawn once and stored. All
three scenarios then run on exactly the same lists. Differences between scenarios can only come from the capacity, not
from one scenario happening to receive sicker patients. In the lab this pairing makes the spread of the estimated
difference between A and B about `r round(b18_sd_ratio, 1)` times smaller than with independent draws.

```{r}
#| label: fig-b18-waits
#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-cap: "Mean waiting time for an operating room per replication (minutes), by triage category and scenario. Each box summarises 200 replications; all scenarios use the same 200 event lists of 14 casualties. A: 2 operating rooms; B: 3 operating rooms; C: 2 operating rooms and a third resuscitation bay. Data status: synthetic."
#| fig-alt: "Box plots in two panels, red patients on the left and yellow patients on the right. In each panel three boxes for scenarios A, B and C show the mean wait for an operating room per replication in minutes. For yellow patients, scenario A has a median around 350 minutes, scenario B around 160 minutes and scenario C slightly above scenario A at about 370 minutes. For red patients the waits are shorter, with medians around 90 minutes in A, about 40 minutes in B and slightly more than A, about 95 minutes, in C. Boxes are distinguished by grey shading and labelled on the horizontal axis."
library(ggplot2)
waits_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(scenario = rep(names(b18_res), each = R_rep), triage = "red",
             wait = unlist(lapply(b18_res, function(m) m[, "wait_or_red"]))),
  data.frame(scenario = rep(names(b18_res), each = R_rep), triage = "yellow",
             wait = unlist(lapply(b18_res, function(m) m[, "wait_or_yellow"])))
)
waits_long$triage <- factor(waits_long$triage, levels = c("red", "yellow"),
                            labels = c("Red (immediate)", "Yellow (urgent)"))
ggplot(waits_long, aes(scenario, wait, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.8, width = 0.6) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", shape = cdsr_shapes[3], size = 2.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ triage) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(A = "grey55", B = "grey90", C = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Scenario (A: 2 ORs; B: 3 ORs; C: 2 ORs + 3rd bay)", y = "Mean wait for an OR (min)",
       caption = "Square: mean over replications. Same 200 synthetic event lists in every scenario.") +
  theme_cdsr()
```

```{r}

#| echo: false
#| purl: false
#| tbl-cap: "Results per scenario over 200 replications with identical event lists (14 casualties each). Waiting times in minutes, mean over replications with the 5th to 95th percentile across replications in brackets. Throughput: operations finished within 6 hours of the alert. Data status: synthetic; all inputs are assumptions."
knitr::kable(b18_table, row.names = FALSE,
             col.names = c("Scenario", "Wait for OR, red", "Wait for OR, yellow", "Wait for bay",
                           "Operations within 6 h", "Last operation ends (h)"))
```

**Which resource limits care here?** In this scenario the operating rooms do. A third operating room roughly halves
the waiting time of yellow patients (from `r round(b18_mean["A", "wait_or_yellow"])` to
`r round(b18_mean["B", "wait_or_yellow"])` minutes on average) and finishes the last operation about
`r round((b18_mean["A", "makespan"] - b18_mean["B", "makespan"]) / 60, 1)` hours earlier. A third resuscitation bay
removes most of the waiting for a bay but does not shorten the wait for an operating room; patients simply reach the
operating room queue sooner and wait there instead. This is the typical behaviour of a system with one binding
constraint: relieving another step moves the queue rather than removing it.

**The most important assumption.** **The comparison holds only for the arrival pattern, treatment times and priority
rules written into the model. The simulation shows the consequences of these assumptions; it does not show that the
real hospital behaves this way.** A published discrete-event model of urban bombing incidents, built from data of 12
incidents, found the resuscitation rooms and the CT scanner, not the operating rooms, to be the main bottlenecks for
critical casualties [@hirshberg1999bombing]. That is not a contradiction. Our model has no CT step and only two bays
with short occupancy; with other assumptions the binding resource changes. A follow-up model defined surge capacity as
a *rate* of critical casualties per hour rather than a number of beds, about 4.6 per hour with immediately available
assets in the studied trauma centre [@hirshberg2005casualty]. Such published figures are useful for a plausibility
check of inputs and outputs, not as a validation of a different hospital.

**Who carries the waiting?** Averages hide the distribution. The priority rule means that yellow patients carry most of
the waiting in every scenario; in scenario A, one in ten replications has a 90th-percentile yellow wait above
`r round(b18_q["A", "p90_yellow_top10"] / 60, 1)` hours. A yellow patient who waits that long may deteriorate, which this
model does not represent. Scenario B has costs that fall outside the model: the elective operations cancelled in the
third room (an *assumption* of four per activation) and a second on-call team that will be tired the next day. A
complete answer to the surgeon names all three groups.

**Question for the workshop:** Your group gets the same event lists but a plan with three bays and three operating
rooms. Before simulating, write down which resource you expect to bind, which patients will carry most of the waiting,
and which group outside the model carries a cost.

## Lab {#sec-b18-lab}

The lab builds the model in five steps: fixed event lists, the model, a verification against a hand calculation, the
scenario runs with checks of resource release, and a summary with variation between runs.

::: {.callout-note title="R start command"}
From the root of the book repository, render the chapter (this runs all code, including the figures of the core
reading):

```bash
quarto render chapters/b18-mass-casualty-capacity-simulation.qmd --to html
```

To run only the Lab code in a fresh R session, start from the `chapters/` folder:

```bash
Rscript -e 'source(knitr::purl("b18-mass-casualty-capacity-simulation.qmd", output = tempfile(fileext = ".R"), quiet = TRUE))'
```

The chapter writes the fixed event lists to `data/b18-event-list.csv`; the same file is the shared input for any
re-implementation.
:::

### Step 1: draw and store the event lists

```{r}
#| label: b18-events
set.seed(1818)
R_rep <- 200                                   # replications
make_events <- function(rep, n = 14) {
  red <- runif(n) < 0.4                        # triage: 40% red (immediate), rest yellow
  data.frame(
    rep = rep, patient = seq_len(n),
    time = round(sort(runif(n, 0, 180)), 1),   # arrival, minutes after alert (3-hour window)
    triage = ifelse(red, "red", "yellow"),
    priority = ifelse(red, 2L, 1L),            # simmer: higher number is served first
    bay_min = round(rlnorm(n, log(30), 0.3), 1),                          # resuscitation bay time
    or_min = round(rlnorm(n, log(ifelse(red, 120, 90)), 0.35), 1)         # operating time
  )
}
events <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(R_rep), make_events))
events_fingerprint <- digest::digest(events)   # checksum: the lists must not change later
head(events, 4)
stopifnot(nrow(events) == R_rep * 14, all(events$bay_min > 0), all(events$or_min > 0))

if (dir.exists("../data")) write.csv(events, "../data/b18-event-list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

### Step 2: the model

Each patient seizes a bay, holds it for the stored bay time, releases it, then seizes an operating room for the stored
operating time. The arrivals come from the stored list (`add_dataframe`), so the model itself draws no random numbers.

```{r}
#| label: b18-model
library(simmer)
run_scenario <- function(ev, n_or, n_bay = 2) {
  env <- simmer("mass-casualty")
  patient <- trajectory("patient") |>
    seize("bay", 1) |>
    timeout_from_attribute("bay_min") |>
    release("bay", 1) |>
    set_attribute("ready_for_or", function() now(env)) |>   # time the patient joins the OR queue
    seize("or", 1) |>
    set_attribute("or_start", function() now(env)) |>
    timeout_from_attribute("or_min") |>
    release("or", 1)
  env |>
    add_resource("bay", capacity = n_bay) |>
    add_resource("or", capacity = n_or) |>
    add_dataframe("p", patient, ev[, c("time", "bay_min", "or_min", "priority")], mon = 2,
                  col_time = "time", time = "absolute",
                  col_attributes = c("bay_min", "or_min"), col_priority = "priority") |>
    run()
}

# one row per patient with waiting times; arrival "p0" is row 1 of the event list
patient_table <- function(env, ev) {
  arr <- get_mon_arrivals(env)
  att <- get_mon_attributes(env)
  att <- att[att$key %in% c("ready_for_or", "or_start"), c("name", "key", "value")]
  att <- reshape(att, idvar = "name", timevar = "key", direction = "wide")
  arr <- merge(arr, att, by = "name")
  arr$row <- as.integer(sub("^p", "", arr$name)) + 1
  arr <- arr[order(arr$row), ]
  arr$triage <- ev$triage[arr$row]
  arr$wait_bay <- round(arr$value.ready_for_or - arr$start_time - ev$bay_min[arr$row], 6)
  arr$wait_or <- round(arr$value.or_start - arr$value.ready_for_or, 6)
  arr
}
```

### Step 3: verification against a hand calculation

Before trusting the model with 200 replications, it must reproduce a case that can be computed on paper. Three patients
arrive at minutes 0, 1 and 2; there is one bay (10 minutes each) and one operating room (60 minutes each). Patient 3 is
red. By hand: patient 1 uses the bay from 0 to 10 and the operating room from 10 to 70 (wait 0). At minute 10 the red
patient 3 jumps the bay queue (bay 10 to 20) and waits for the operating room from 20 to 70 (wait 50). Patient 2 uses
the bay from 20 to 30 and waits until patient 3 is finished at 130 (wait 100).

```{r}
#| label: b18-checks
hand <- data.frame(time = c(0, 1, 2), bay_min = 10, or_min = 60, priority = c(1L, 1L, 2L),
                   triage = c("yellow", "yellow", "red"))
hand_env <- run_scenario(hand, n_or = 1, n_bay = 1)
hand_tab <- patient_table(hand_env, hand)
hand_tab[, c("name", "triage", "start_time", "value.ready_for_or", "value.or_start", "wait_or", "end_time")]
stopifnot(all(hand_tab$wait_or == c(0, 100, 50)),     # hand calculation
          all(hand_tab$end_time == c(70, 190, 130)))
```

### Step 4: run the scenarios and check resource release

For every run, four checks are made: every patient finished; arrival times equal the stored list; at the end both
resources are free and their queues empty (no patient kept a resource it should have released); and the area under
the operating-room queue-length curve equals the sum of all individual waits for an operating room. The last check is
an exact accounting identity behind Little's law [@little1961queuing]: time spent waiting, counted per patient or
counted per minute of queue, must be the same.

```{r}
#| label: b18-run
run_metrics <- function(ev, n_or, n_bay = 2) {
  env <- run_scenario(ev, n_or, n_bay)
  a <- patient_table(env, ev)
  r <- get_mon_resources(env)
  r <- r[order(r$time), ]
  final <- aggregate(cbind(server, queue) ~ resource, r, function(x) tail(x, 1))
  r_or <- r[r$resource == "or", ]
  queue_area <- sum(head(r_or$queue, -1) * diff(r_or$time))   # integral of OR queue length
  stopifnot(nrow(a) == nrow(ev), all(a$finished),               # everyone finished
            isTRUE(all.equal(a$start_time, ev$time)),           # inputs used unchanged
            all(final$server == 0), all(final$queue == 0),      # resources released
            isTRUE(all.equal(queue_area, sum(a$wait_or))))      # accounting identity
  c(wait_or_red = mean(a$wait_or[a$triage == "red"]),
    wait_or_yellow = mean(a$wait_or[a$triage == "yellow"]),
    p90_yellow = unname(quantile(a$wait_or[a$triage == "yellow"], 0.9)),
    wait_bay = mean(a$wait_bay),
    done_6h = sum(a$end_time <= 360),
    makespan = max(a$end_time))
}
scenarios <- list(A = c(n_or = 2, n_bay = 2), B = c(n_or = 3, n_bay = 2), C = c(n_or = 2, n_bay = 3))
# lists with no yellow patient give NaN for yellow waits; they are kept and reported
b18_res <- lapply(scenarios, function(s)
  t(sapply(seq_len(R_rep), function(r) run_metrics(events[events$rep == r, ], s["n_or"], s["n_bay"]))))
stopifnot(identical(digest::digest(events), events_fingerprint))   # same events in every scenario

b18_mean <- t(sapply(b18_res, colMeans, na.rm = TRUE))
b18_q <- t(sapply(b18_res, function(m) c(apply(m, 2, quantile, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                                          p90_yellow_top10 = unname(quantile(m[, "p90_yellow"], 0.9, na.rm = TRUE)))))
fmt <- function(s, v, d = 0) sprintf("%s (%s–%s)", round(b18_mean[s, v], d),
                                       round(quantile(b18_res[[s]][, v], 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), d),
                                       round(quantile(b18_res[[s]][, v], 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), d))
b18_table <- data.frame(
  scenario = c("A: 2 ORs, 2 bays", "B: 3 ORs, 2 bays", "C: 2 ORs, 3 bays"),
  red = sapply(names(scenarios), fmt, v = "wait_or_red"),
  yellow = sapply(names(scenarios), fmt, v = "wait_or_yellow"),
  bay = sapply(names(scenarios), fmt, v = "wait_bay"),
  done = sapply(names(scenarios), fmt, v = "done_6h", d = 1),
  last = sapply(names(scenarios), function(s) sprintf("%.1f", b18_mean[s, "makespan"] / 60))
)
round(b18_mean, 1)

# statements made in the core reading
stopifnot(b18_mean["B", "wait_or_yellow"] < 0.6 * b18_mean["A", "wait_or_yellow"],  # third OR helps
          b18_mean["C", "wait_bay"] < 0.5 * b18_mean["A", "wait_bay"],               # third bay removes bay waits
          b18_mean["C", "wait_or_yellow"] >= b18_mean["A", "wait_or_yellow"])        # ... but not OR waits
```

### Step 5: variation between runs, paired and unpaired

The table in the core reading reports the spread across replications. The more important spread for the decision is
that of the *difference* between scenarios. With paired event lists, each replication gives one difference B minus A
for the same 14 patients. For comparison, scenario B is also run on a second, independent set of event lists.

```{r}
#| label: b18-pairing
diff_paired <- b18_res$B[, "wait_or_yellow"] - b18_res$A[, "wait_or_yellow"]
set.seed(1819)
events_independent <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(R_rep), make_events))
res_B_independent <- t(sapply(seq_len(R_rep), function(r)
  run_metrics(events_independent[events_independent$rep == r, ], n_or = 3)))
diff_unpaired <- res_B_independent[, "wait_or_yellow"] - b18_res$A[, "wait_or_yellow"]
b18_sd <- c(paired = sd(diff_paired, na.rm = TRUE), unpaired = sd(diff_unpaired, na.rm = TRUE))
b18_sd_ratio <- unname(b18_sd["unpaired"] / b18_sd["paired"])
round(c(mean_paired = mean(diff_paired, na.rm = TRUE), b18_sd, ratio = b18_sd_ratio), 1)
stopifnot(b18_sd["paired"] < b18_sd["unpaired"],
          mean(diff_paired < 0, na.rm = TRUE) > 0.95)   # B shortens the yellow wait in almost every list
```

With paired lists, scenario B shortens the mean yellow wait in
`r cdsr_percent(mean(diff_paired < 0, na.rm = TRUE))` of replications, by
`r round(-mean(diff_paired, na.rm = TRUE))` minutes on average. The standard deviation of the difference is
`r round(b18_sd["paired"])` minutes with paired lists and `r round(b18_sd["unpaired"])` minutes with independent
lists. Pairing does not change what the model assumes; it removes noise that has nothing to do with the question.

::: {.callout-note title="Other implementation: SimPy"}
**Original implementation.** SimPy, a process-based discrete-event simulation library for Python [@simpy], version
4.1.2 (current release on the Python Package Index, accessed 8 November 2026);
[documentation](https://simpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/).

**Concrete advantage.** Each patient is written as a Python generator function, so interruptions, pre-emption and
re-triage can be followed line by line in the program flow. Teams with an existing Python data pipeline can keep the
simulation in the same environment.

**What must be identical for a fair comparison.** The input file `data/b18-event-list.csv` (arrival, triage, bay and
operating times per replication), the capacities, and the priority rule. Note the direction: in `simmer` a *higher*
priority number is served first, in SimPy's `PriorityResource` a *lower* number is. Ties are resolved by the time of
the request in SimPy; check that equal arrival times are ordered the same way. Compare the event log (order of starts
and ends) first, then the waiting times. Tolerance: identical event order and waiting times equal up to floating-point
rounding (10⁻⁶ minutes). The same seed in R and Python does not produce the same random draws, which is why the event
list is exchanged as a file rather than regenerated.

**Status.** Conceptual comparison, not executed. No statement about speed is made.
:::

## Counter-check {#sec-b18-countercheck}

Scenario C, the third resuscitation bay, is the counter-check. Before looking at the numbers, predict: will the mean
wait for a bay go up or down? Will the mean wait for an operating room go up, down or stay the same? Then compare with
the code output.

```{r}
#| label: b18-countercheck
round(rbind(A = b18_mean["A", c("wait_bay", "wait_or_red", "wait_or_yellow", "makespan")],
            C = b18_mean["C", c("wait_bay", "wait_or_red", "wait_or_yellow", "makespan")]), 1)
stopifnot(abs(b18_mean["C", "makespan"] - b18_mean["A", "makespan"]) < 15)  # last operation hardly moves
```

The wait for a bay falls from `r round(b18_mean["A", "wait_bay"])` to `r round(b18_mean["C", "wait_bay"])` minutes,
but the wait for an operating room does not fall; for yellow patients it rises slightly
(`r round(b18_mean["A", "wait_or_yellow"])` to `r round(b18_mean["C", "wait_or_yellow"])` minutes), because patients
now reach the operating room queue earlier and wait there instead, while the two operating rooms work through the same
caseload at the same pace. The time until the last operation ends hardly changes. In this scenario the third bay buys comfort in the emergency department, not earlier surgery.
Change one more assumption yourself: shorten the bay time to 15 minutes, or add a CT step with one scanner, and check
whether the binding resource moves.

## Consequences for patients and operations {#sec-b18-consequences}

**Ethics.** A triage rule is a value judgement about who waits. The model makes its consequences visible: in every
scenario yellow patients carry most of the waiting, and the model does not represent deterioration while waiting, which
would turn some yellow patients red. Capacity decisions also distribute burdens outside the model: elective patients
whose operations are cancelled, and the on-call team that works through the night. A mass casualty plan that reports
only the mean waiting time of casualties leaves these groups out; @sec-b21 discusses how to make such trade-offs
explicit.

**Reporting and validity.** Simulation studies should report inputs, their sources, the handling of random numbers,
the number of replications and the verification steps; the STRESS guidelines give a checklist [@monks2019stress]. A
plan based on a simulation should state which inputs were assumptions and which came from local data, and when they
will be checked against the next exercise or real incident.

**Regulation.** Indirect. A planning simulation for a mass casualty plan has no medical purpose for an individual
patient. The question changes if software is used during an incident to assign individual patients to operating rooms
or to set treatment priority. Systems for emergency healthcare patient triage are listed as high-risk uses in Annex III,
point 5(d), of the AI Act [@eu2024aiact]; for such a use the questions of @sec-b22 apply. As of November 2026.

**Data protection and security.** Treatment times derived from the hospital's operating-room records are health data
when they are linked to persons; for the model, aggregated distributions per procedure group are sufficient. During a
real incident, the plan must work if scheduling software is unavailable; a printed version of the decision rules is
part of the fallback (@sec-b24).

## Look up and transfer {#sec-b18-lookup}

- **Reviewer question:** Were the scenarios compared on identical input events, how many replications were run, how
  was the model verified, and which inputs are local data and which are assumptions?
- **Self-test:** A team compares two and three operating rooms with 50 replications per scenario. Each scenario uses its
  own random seed. They report mean yellow waits of 410 and 200 minutes with overlapping 95% intervals across
  replications and conclude that "the difference is uncertain". What would you change in the design and in the report?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Draw the event lists once and run both scenarios on the same lists (common random numbers). Report the distribution of
the paired differences per replication, for example the mean difference with its 5th and 95th percentiles and the share
of replications in which three rooms are better. Overlapping intervals of two separate means are the wrong comparison:
most of their width comes from differences between event lists, which affect both scenarios alike. Also report the
waits of red and yellow patients separately and name the costs outside the model (cancelled elective operations, staff).
:::

- **Annotated sources:**
  - @ucar2019simmer describe `simmer`, the discrete-event simulation package used in the lab; the
    [simmer website](https://r-simmer.org/) documents `add_dataframe()` and the monitoring functions.
  - @sargent2013validation summarises verification and validation of simulation models, including the difference
    between checking the model logic and checking the model against reality.
  - @monks2019stress (STRESS) provide reporting guidelines for simulation studies.
  - @hirshberg1999bombing built a discrete-event model of hospital resources in urban bombing incidents and found
    resuscitation rooms and CT, not operating rooms, to be the bottlenecks for critical casualties.
  - @hirshberg2005casualty related casualty load to the level of trauma care and expressed surge capacity as a rate
    of critical casualties per hour.
  - @little1961queuing proved the queuing formula L = λW, which underlies the accounting check in step 4.
  - @simpy is the documentation of SimPy for the comparison box.

In W6 (teaching unit 22, station "mass casualty") learners simulate paired arrival sequences for two capacity
scenarios and hand in a waiting-time distribution with its spread across runs. The project work in teaching unit 24
uses the same structure: model, baseline scenario and one counter-check that another group reproduces from a fresh R
session.
